lead: Light is an oscillating electric and magnetic field travelling through space. Its colour, and the energy it can deliver to a molecule, are fixed by one number: frequency. Matter absorbs a photon only when the photon energy matches the gap between two allowed levels. This single rule explains why some solutions look coloured, why IR spectra identify functional groups, and why sunlight drives photochemistry. It also sets the design of every spectrometer, from a ₹15,000 school colorimeter to a hospital MRI scanner.
prereq: You need Unit 1, Chemical Bonding and Coordination Compounds: wave–particle duality, photon energy E = hν, and the idea of quantized levels.

sections.h3: Wave parameters: λ, ν, c and wavenumber

blocks.text: Electromagnetic (EM) radiation is a travelling wave with an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. The wavelength λ is the distance between successive crests, measured in metres (m) or nanometres (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m). The frequency ν is the number of oscillations per second, in hertz (1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹).
In vacuum all EM waves travel at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The three quantities are linked by c = νλ. Because c is fixed, λ and ν move in opposite directions: a short wavelength means a high frequency.

blocks.where: ν is frequency in Hz; λ is wavelength in m; c is the speed of light in vacuum, 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

blocks.text: Wavenumber ν̃ is the number of waves in one centimetre: ν̃ = 1/λ when λ is in cm. It is a reciprocal length, in cm⁻¹, not a length. IR spectra use 4000–400 cm⁻¹ because the numbers are convenient and proportional to energy. Higher ν̃ means higher frequency and higher photon energy.

blocks.where: λ is wavelength in cm; ν̃ is wavenumber in cm⁻¹.

blocks.text: The EM family runs from radio waves (λ of metres) through microwaves, infrared, visible (about 400–700 nm), ultraviolet, X-rays, to gamma rays (λ below 10⁻¹¹ m). X-rays and gamma rays are ionizing. Radiofrequency flips nuclear spins in NMR (Chapter 2.6); microwaves rotate molecules (Chapter 2.5); infrared excites vibrations (Chapter 2.4); visible and UV excite electrons (Chapter 2.3).

sections.h3: Photon energy and the matching condition

blocks.text: Light also behaves as a stream of photons. One photon carries energy E = hν, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is Planck's constant. Using c = νλ gives E = hc/λ. In electronvolts, E(eV) ≈ 1240/λ(nm). At 500 nm, E ≈ 2.48 eV.

blocks.where: E is photon energy in J; h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; ν is frequency in Hz; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; λ is wavelength in m.

blocks.text: A molecule has discrete energy levels. It absorbs a photon only when the photon energy equals the gap: hν = ΔE = E_upper − E_lower. The photon disappears and the molecule is promoted. Emission is the reverse. This is one-photon absorption; two-photon processes need much higher intensity and are not the usual case.

A matching gap is necessary but not sufficient. Selection rules, set by symmetry and conserved angular momentum, decide whether a transition is allowed. A simple harmonic oscillator absorbs IR only with Δv = ±1; a rigid rotor absorbs microwaves with ΔJ = ±1; electronic transitions usually keep spin, ΔS = 0. 'Forbidden' lines can appear weakly when rules break down.

Intensity is different from photon energy. Intensity counts photons per second per unit area. A brighter beam excites more molecules, but each photon still has E = hν. Bright red light (about 700 nm, 1.8 eV) cannot cross a 3 eV gap, however intense it is. Absorbance, the quantity measured in a colorimeter, is covered in Chapter 2.2.

An absorption spectrum is a plot of radiation missing after passing through a sample. Each dip or line sits at a frequency whose photon energy matches a gap. An emission spectrum shows the frequencies given out when excited species fall back. Line position gives the gap; line strength depends on the number of absorbing molecules, the population difference and the transition probability.

No spectral line is infinitely sharp. Natural lifetime broadening comes from the uncertainty relation ΔE Δt ≥ ħ/2, where ħ = h/2π: a short-lived excited state has a poorly defined energy. Collisions and pressure broaden lines in gases and liquids. Doppler motion broadens lines in hot gases. Instrument resolution adds its own width. Broadening carries information about lifetime, temperature and environment, so it is measured, not merely ignored.

The same one-photon rule underlies UV-visible, IR and NMR spectra, but each technique probes a different kind of gap. Photochemistry begins after absorption: only absorbed photons can drive reaction (Chapter 2.8). Some syllabi call this topic interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter; the essential content is the matching condition plus selection rules.

figure.caption: Photon energy falls as wavelength rises; at 500 nm it is 2.48 eV. The curve is E = 1240/λ with λ in nm.

spec.aria: A plot of photon energy in electronvolts against wavelength in nanometres; the marked point at 500 nm has energy 2.48 eV.

examples.question: A green laser pointer used in a classroom has wavelength 500 nm. (a) Find the photon energy in joules. (b) Convert it to electronvolts. (c) Find the wavenumber in cm⁻¹. Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
steps: Convert wavelength: λ = 500 nm = 500 × 10⁻⁹ m = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m.
Write the photon-energy formula: E = hc/λ.
Convert to electronvolts: E = 3.9756 × 10⁻¹⁹ J / 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ = 2.4816 eV ≈ 2.48 eV. This agrees with 1240/500 = 2.48.
Convert wavelength to cm: λ = 500 × 10⁻⁷ cm = 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ cm. Then ν̃ = 1/λ = 1/(5.00 × 10⁻⁵ cm) = 2.00 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹.
examples.answer: The 500 nm photon has energy 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or 2.48 eV, and the wavenumber is 2.00 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹.
examples.check:
h = 6.626e-34
c = 3.00e8
lam_nm = 500
lam_m = lam_nm * 1e-9
E = h * c / lam_m
eV = E / 1.602e-19
wn = 1 / (lam_m * 100)
print(f"{E:.2e}")
print(f"{eV:.2f}")
print(f"{wn:.2e}")

traps: Using λ = 500 in E = hc/λ without converting nanometres to metres gives an answer 10⁹ times too small.
For wavenumber, convert to cm first: 500 nm is 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ cm, so ν̃ = 2.00 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹. Wavenumber is reciprocal length, not a length; a larger wavenumber means a shorter wavelength.
Energy and wavelength move oppositely, while frequency and energy move together. A 400 nm photon carries more energy than a 700 nm photon.
Bright light is not automatically high-energy light: intensity changes the photon count, not hν. A 500 nm photon is not ionizing.
A matched energy gap does not guarantee strong absorption; selection rules can make a transition weak or forbidden.

quiz.q: Define wavelength, frequency and wavenumber, with units.
quiz.a: Wavelength λ is crest-to-crest distance (m or nm). Frequency ν is oscillations per second (Hz = s⁻¹). Wavenumber ν̃ is 1/λ with λ in cm, in cm⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why can a 500 nm photon not ionize a molecule that needs 5 eV?
quiz.a: Its energy is 1240/500 ≈ 2.48 eV, below the 5 eV gap. A single photon of this energy cannot supply the difference.

quiz.q: Find the photon energy of 400 nm light in eV.
Find the wavenumber of 10 μm radiation in cm⁻¹.
Two beams have equal power but wavelengths 400 nm and 700 nm. Which delivers more photons per second, and why?
quiz.a: The 700 nm beam. Each 700 nm photon has lower energy (1.77 eV versus 3.10 eV), so more photons are needed to make the same power.

quiz.q: A gas absorption line becomes wider when pressure rises. Suggest a reason.
quiz.a: More frequent collisions shorten the excited-state lifetime or perturb energy levels. By ΔE Δt ≥ ħ/2, a shorter lifetime gives a larger energy spread, so the line broadens.

quiz.q: Why do IR spectroscopists quote wavenumber rather than wavelength?
quiz.a: Wavenumber is proportional to photon energy and gives convenient whole-number ranges, such as 4000–400 cm⁻¹, without tiny metre values.

beyond: Not for the exam. Astronomical spectra use the same lines to measure stellar composition and redshift. Remote sensing satellites identify gases by their IR fingerprints. Telecom engineers choose wavelengths where glass fibres absorb least. Quantum technologies use single photons at well-defined energies.
